articleTitle: Car alarms-origins to present systems and future trends
abstract: The author examines car alarm systems by reviewing early security devices and tracing their subsequent development into today's relatively sophisticated equipment. He concludes by presenting possible future trends in the field of automobile security.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Biometrics is the application of mathematical and statistical methods to the study of biology. In recent years the technology has been applied to the machine identification of humans from a personal trait or characteristic. It is probably more accurate to describe the aims of the technology as the verification of an identity because a statistically based system will provide only a probability that the individual is who he or she claims to be. The authors argue that vehicle manufacturers could benefit considerably from the development and application of this technology to their products as it provides their customers with a secure biometric access control key for initially their vehicle, subsequently their home, office etc.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Opportunities exist for organised criminals to open vehicles fitted with remote locking systems, by listening for the key code, storing the code and retransmitting it, such a device being known as a keygrabber. In this paper, fundamental requirements are developed for key encoders which both maintain synchronism with their decoder and can be guaranteed to evade keygrabbers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

The author describes the construction of a security concept car by the Rover Group to highlight automobile protection. The car chosen to be the basis for the concept car was a Rover Sterling saloon which already had several useful security features: bonded glass for all fixed glazing; twin bonnet latches; sturdy trunk latch; and an anti-syphon device in the fuel tank. Additionally over thirty security features were added to the car under the four headings: physical exterior security; alarm system; vehicle immobilisation; and reduced desirability to a thief.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

It is now possible to install in a motor vehicle a low cost computer system with a large memory housed in quite an insignificant black box. The authors examine to what extent, if provided with the necessary sensors, can such a system log data of the vehicle's position so that an accurate map can subsequently be drawn of the vehicle's route? A successful route logger of this kind if it did not deter thieves might well provide sufficient evidence to convict them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

In November 1985, committees were established in the UK to consider as initial projects the production of standards for car alarms and car locks. By the very nature of things the consideration of car locks was taken into the motor manufacturers association, and that of alarms by a wider spread of interests ranging from the vehicle producers, the specialist alarm makers, the police crime prevention unit, insurers and not least vehicle users. Here, the author examines the work of these committees and offers an insight into future European standards with the advent of the single market in 1992.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sensing systems and procedures for theft alarm systems
abstract: The break-ins and thefts in the sector of motor cars are increasing in an alarming way. More than 55% of car breaks are carried out by smashing, removing or forcing open a window. Here the author details various protection techniques, including ultrasonic and infrared methods, which could be adapted to automobile security systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

What is a smart card? It is a credit card with a small microprocessor chip with more information and with more ability to talk back to its interrogator than a credit card. Its scope is increasing daily as the development of the microchip produces more power in a smaller space and with the use of less power. However clever, a device needs to be used and given clear instructions to use its capability properly. The author discusses the various problems and system design which can flow from the versatile ability of the smart card. In particular, he examines the application of such technology to the field of automobile security systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
